quadHead: Four ways Colombia catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: The Playa Blanca Service Ambush
quad.tl: A vendor brings an unrequested taste of ceviche, then an unpriced massage, then a piña colada nobody quoted — and at the end of the afternoon hands you a bill for 2,000,000 COP. Your boat back leaves in twenty minutes; that pressure is the part you are paying for. Agree on every price before anything touches your hands.

quad.title: Express Taxi Kidnapping (Paseo Millonario)
quad.tl: You hail a yellow taxi outside a Chapinero restaurant at 11 PM. Two minutes in, the cab stops at a red light, two men climb in beside you, and for the next three hours they drive you between ATMs draining the daily cap on every card you own. Use a trusted app, never a flagged-down street taxi after dark.

quad.title: The Fake-Emerald Swindle
quad.tl: A shop near Plaza de Bolívar shows a calculator reading 155,000 COP for a small silver necklace and stone, you tap your card, and the receipt comes through for 500,000 COP — and the “Colombian emerald” appraises back home as near-worthless glass. Emerald row runs on opaque pricing and unverified stones; no certificate, no deal.

quad.title: Fake-Police Drug-Search Shakedown
quad.tl: A stranger off the Comuna 13 stairs offers cocaine; you wave him off, and ten seconds later two men in untucked polo shirts flash a laminated badge and demand to “inspect” your wallet for the marked bills they say you just handled. The badges are fake and the dealer is in on it — real police never search your wallet for cash on the street.

body: Colombia: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Colombian police and consumer-agency sources — the Policía Nacional (123), the Policía de Turismo and the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC) — plus r/ColombiaTravel reports and verified Colombian press. Sourced, not recycled.

58 specific scams across Bogotá, Medellín, Cartagena, Cali, Santa Marta and five more destinations. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Spanish phrases that shut them down — in plain Spanish you can show on your phone, with the steps to file a denuncia if it has already happened.
Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched and updated every year — the current edition lives in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Colombia relaxed, not braced.
